title: Block 3 ISGL Questions
context: Foundations of Medicine, Block 3, ISGL sessions

questions.p: Sarah's illness is linked to her camping trip. She also worked in a chemistry lab over the summer. Which environmental factor best explains her risk?
o: UV exposure from long days spent camping
Pesticide spraying in the park
Solvent exposure in her summer lab job
Warmer temperatures expanding tick range
questions.e:
Correct: D. Warmer temperatures expand tick range, which is the climate link in her Lyme disease.
A: UV exposure is a separate environmental topic and does not cause tick-borne illness.
B: Pesticides are a separate environmental topic in the module.
C: The lab solvents are a distractor in this case.
Takeaway: Climate change drives the spread of vector-borne disease.

questions.p: Sarah is diagnosed with Lyme disease. Which statement about her diagnosis is correct?
o: It is not reportable after one case
It is reportable only if she is admitted
It is reportable to public health
It is reportable only by her own doctor
questions.e:
Correct: C. Lyme disease is a disease of public health significance, so it is reportable.
A: Its status as a disease of public health significance makes each case reportable.
B: Its status as a disease of public health significance makes it reportable, not the care setting.
D: Reporting follows the disease, not which doctor made the diagnosis.
Takeaway: Know what "disease of public health significance" means for your duty to report.

questions.p: Mrs. Haddad, 52, arrived in Canada 3 months ago and speaks limited English. Her 14-year-old son offers to interpret at her visit for back pain. What is the best approach?
o: Book a professional interpreter
Speak slowly and give an English handout
Rely on gestures and a pain scale
Let her son interpret for the visit
questions.e:
Correct: A. For a newcomer with limited English, use a professional interpreter, not family. Speak plainly and use teach-back.
B: A handout in English does not overcome the language barrier.
C: Gestures cannot confirm she understands. Teach-back through an interpreter can.
D: Family members should not interpret.
Takeaway: Underrepresented groups need the plan fitted to their reality, including language.

questions.p: Your classmate Dev has gone quiet in small group, skips social events and deflects every compliment. He is anxious even before low-stakes quizzes. He shows no signs of depression or safety concerns. What is the best first step?
o: Report your concerns to the faculty right away
Check in with him privately and listen first
Wait to see whether he raises it with you
Tell him his grades prove he is doing fine
questions.e:
Correct: B. Going quiet, skipping events, deflecting compliments and anxiety over low-stakes tasks are signs a peer is struggling. Start with a private, casual check-in and listen before trying to fix it.
A: Escalation to LEO or a faculty member is for signs of depression or safety concerns.
C: Waiting leaves the pattern unnamed. The approach starts with you checking in.
D: Pointing out evidence of competence comes after you listen and normalize the feeling.
Takeaway: Supports for students: the Schulich Learner Experience Office, Western Wellness, mentors and peer support.

questions.p: Samantha, a first-year medical student, spends every night before a formative quiz over-preparing. She passes with a high mark. Following the imposter cycle, which step comes next?
o: She credits the result to luck or effort
Her anxiety before the next quiz fades
She accepts the praise from her peers
She asks a trusted mentor for extra support
questions.e:
Correct: A. The imposter cycle runs task, anxiety, over-preparing or procrastinating, success, then credit goes to luck or effort. Praise is then discounted and the fraud feeling grows.
B: The fraud feeling grows, so the next task brings more anxiety.
C: Praise gets discounted in the cycle, not accepted.
D: Seeking support is a way out of the cycle, not one of its steps.
Takeaway: Imposter syndrome is an inaccurate self-assessment, closely tied to perfectionism.

questions.p: Which statement about implicit bias is correct?
o: It is driven mainly by slow, deliberate System 2
Implicit attitudes improved as fast as explicit attitudes
Holding it means a person is racist or sexist
It acts most under fatigue, hunger and time pressure
questions.e:
Correct: D. Implicit bias has its strongest effect under fatigue, stress, hunger, time pressure and heavy cognitive load.
A: Fast, automatic System 1 steers most behaviour.
B: Explicit attitudes improved over decades, but implicit attitudes have not.
C: Having bias does not make you racist or sexist. It is a normal brain shortcut.
Takeaway: Implicit bias often clashes with your stated beliefs.

questions.p:
Which are career consequences of untreated imposter syndrome in a physician?
i) Burnout from over-preparing
ii) Hiding uncertainty in a way that puts patient safety at risk
iii) Turning down leadership roles
iv) Responding to errors with learning instead of shame
o: i) and iii) only
ii), iii) and iv) only
i), ii) and iii) only
All of the above
questions.e:
Correct: C. Over-preparing leads to burnout, hiding uncertainty and not asking for help puts patient safety at risk, and affected physicians turn down leadership roles or competitive specialties.
A: This leaves out the patient safety risk from hiding uncertainty.
B: Statement iv) is reversed. Imposter syndrome makes you respond to errors with shame.
D: Statement iv) is reversed.
Takeaway: It also weakens teaching and raises the risk of anxiety and depression.

questions.p: Andrea, 34, is a PSW on probation with no work benefits. She hurt her back lifting a patient during her shift. She is 2 weeks into the job and worried about missing work. Which resource best covers her physio, drugs and lost wages?
o: OHIP-funded community physio
A WSIB claim for a work injury
The Trillium Drug Program
Employment Insurance sickness benefits
questions.e:
Correct: B. Her injury happened at work, so a WSIB claim covers physio, drugs and lost wages.
A: OHIP physio is for those 19 and under, 65 and over, after a recent hospital stay or day surgery, or on OW or ODSP. She fits none.
C: Trillium helps with high drug costs relative to income, with an income-based deductible. It does not cover physio or wages.
D: EI sickness benefits replace some income only, not physio or drugs.
Takeaway: Ask whether the injury started at work. It opens the door to WSIB.

questions.p: Dr. Lee sees a frustrated patient who waited 3 hours. She says, "If I were in your shoes, I might feel ignored. Am I close?" Which of van Ryn's strategies to reduce bias is she using?
o: Perspective-taking
Counter-stereotypic contact
Protecting cognitive resources
Partnership-building
questions.e:
Correct: A. Perspective-taking means picturing the visit from the patient's side, then checking it with them.
B: Counter-stereotypic contact is a separate strategy from Capatosto, not one of van Ryn's three.
C: Protecting cognitive resources means sleep, food, stress control and fixing system pressures.
D: Partnership-building uses "we" and "let's" and names shared goals.
Takeaway: van Ryn's 3 strategies: perspective-taking, partnership-building, protecting cognitive resources.

questions.p: Sarah, 21, has fever and tender right groin nodes for 1 week, with possible mild splenomegaly. She has a 5 cm circular red rash on the back of her upper leg. She went camping at Pinery Provincial Park 2 weeks ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cat scratch disease
Lyme disease
Lymphoma of the groin nodes
Infectious mononucleosis
questions.e:
Correct: B. A circular rash after camping, with fever, points to Lyme disease. The rash is erythema migrans, and Pinery is a known tick area in Ontario.
A: Cat scratch disease is on the differential, but she has no cat exposure.
C: Lymphoma is on the differential, but it does not explain the rash after camping.
D: Mono is on the differential, but it does not explain the circular rash.
Takeaway: Fever with lymphadenopathy has a wide differential: mono, cat scratch, STIs, lymphoma, local skin infection.
